sources.title: A. M. Chowdhury, Pala Dynasty, Banglapedia (Asiatic Society of Bangladesh)
sources.note: Full indexed original read; direct page extraction failed. Used for mid-eighth-century foundation, varying imperial fortunes, Sena displacement and uncertain relationship of later Bihar namesakes. Rhetorical claims of superiority are not adopted.

sources.title: DHARMA: Khalimpur Plate of Dharmapāla, year 32, edited by Amandine Wattelier-Bricout and Arlo Griffiths
sources.note: Direct edition and translation read. Verses 12 and 13 are royal praise, not independent confirmation of the scale of conquests or universal popularity. Sanskrit in Siddhamatrika script.

sources.title: DHARMA: Nalanda Plate of Devapāla, year 35, edited by Ryosuke Furui and Arlo Griffiths
sources.note: Direct scholarly edition and translation read. Seal line 1 provides exact Roman transliteration and gloss. Modern reading is year 35, rather than the older year 39. Lines 33 to 42 describe five villages, Balaputradeva request, monastic provisions, medical fund and fiscal obligations.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Ruins of the Buddhist Vihara at Paharpur
sources.note: Direct description and Statement of Outstanding Universal Value read. The 177 cells belong to the final building phase; not an enrollment figure. Monument developed over centuries.

sources.title: Archaeological Survey of India: Excavations at Paharpur, Bengal, page 29
sources.note: Original excavation report, indexed page 29 read through exact site query. Direct PDF fetch failed. Cooking hall identification and kitchen/refectory use of wells are archaeological interpretations, retained as such. Ashes in the long refectory also indicate a fire; kitchen ashes are the separate western building evidence.

sources.title: Archaeological Survey of India: Annual Report, Exploration at Paharpur, page 127
sources.note: Indexed original page 127 read through exact query for gargoyle and mouth. Direct PDF fetch failed. Channels under antechambers and circumambulation passage, mouth outlet and onward masonry drain described explicitly; no toilet identification inferred.

sources.title: Ashok Bhattacharyya, Pala Painting, Banglapedia (Asiatic Society of Bangladesh)
sources.note: Direct article read. Uses technical preparation of palm leaves, pigment list, and manuscript dedications to parents and teachers. Inconsistent regnal dates and unqualified dynastic claims elsewhere in this article are not used.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Green Tara, leaf from an Ashtasahasrika Prajnaparamita manuscript
sources.note: Direct object record read. Twelfth century, Bihar or West Bengal, ink and color on palm leaf, 5.1 by 55.6 cm.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: The Buddha Giving Safety to Mariners
sources.note: Direct object record read. About 1090, Bengal or Bangladesh; religious imagery of marine protection and a lower scene with a vina. The possible identification of one deity as Rahu is omitted.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Portrait of the Indian Monk Atisha
sources.note: Direct curatorial text and metadata read. Atisha at Vikramashila and 1042 journey; portrait is early to mid-twelfth-century Tibet, not a contemporary Pala court portrait. Specific inviting king name omitted.

proposedOverrides.name: Pala Empire
proposedOverrides.summary: Bengal and Bihar’s imperial dynasty, renowned for Buddhist learning and manuscript arts.

batchIdentityNotes.historicalScope: Imperial Palas of Bengal and Bihar, founded in the mid-eighth century, losing Bengal to Sena expansion in the twelfth. Not the separate Pala dynasty of Kamarupa. Late Bihar rulers with Pala names are not assumed proven imperial descendants.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: Decoded snapshots begin at 700 with bbox 83.983, 19.606, 91.684, 26.450. Maximum east extent reaches 93.412 in 800 and 900; 1000 and 1100 repeat a broad outline ending 91.439, 27.313. Polygon is a coarse imported regional envelope, not evidence of uninterrupted authority throughout it.
batchIdentityNotes.sourceLimits: Politics from Asiatic Society specialist entry and royal charters read as praise. Everyday detail is mainly monastic/elite evidence, not a universal family reconstruction. Excavation reports have indexed-original access, not locally downloaded full PDFs. The writing sample is an exact attested scholarly transliteration, not reconstructed original glyphs.
